title: Chemical Homogeneity as a Key Factor in the Martensitic Transformation of Powder-Metallurgically Processed X2CrNi18-9 Steel: Implications for Hydrogen Embrittlement
abstract: Abstract Austenitic stainless steels produced by powder metallurgy (PM) reportedly exhibit higher resistance to hydrogen embrittlement than conventionally produced grades. This improved resistance is commonly attributed to their lower tendency for martensitic phase transformation. One previously unaddressed factor that may contribute to this behavior is the difference in chemical homogeneity between PM and conventionally manufactured parts. The present work investigates chemical homogeneity as a factor influencing the phase stability of PM-produced metastable austenitic steel X2CrNi18-9. Slow strain rate tensile tests were conducted at − 50 °C on cast and hot-formed (wrought) specimens, as well as on PM conditions produced by hot isostatic pressing and PBF-LB/M. Simultaneous electron backscatter diffraction and energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry of the wrought material reveal band-like Ni and Cr segregations elongated along the deformation direction. Ni-depleted regions were identified as preferential sites for martensite formation, which propagates in a block-like manner into regions of higher austenite stability. In contrast, the PM conditions exhibit higher chemical homogeneity, resulting in an overall lower fraction of deformation-induced martensite. This study demonstrates that chemical homogeneity is a critical parameter in the assessment of hydrogen embrittlement resistance of austenitic stainless steels and should be considered alongside other influencing factors.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) poses a significant challenge in the design and long-term reliability of metallic components, particularly in energy, transportation, and chemical processing industries. The ingress of hydrogen into metals can lead to premature failure through cracking and loss of ductility, especially under mechanical stress. [ 1 , 2 ]  As hydrogen technologies, such as fuel cells and hydrogen storage systems, become increasingly prominent in the pursuit of carbon-neutral energy solutions, understanding and mitigating hydrogen-induced degradation in structural materials is of growing technical importance.

In hydrogen-related technologies, components such as piping, valves, and fasteners are primarily made of steel due to its favorable mechanical properties and ease of fabrication. [ 3 ]  These components are often exposed to hydrogen-rich environments, making them susceptible to HE. To mitigate this risk, materials with inherently high resistance to HE must be used. High-alloy austenitic stainless steels are particularly well suited for such applications, primarily due to their high ductility and low hydrogen diffusivity. Among these, steels within the compositional range of AISI 316L—such as X2CrNiMo18-14-3 (DIN EN 1.4435)—have been established as standard materials for components operating in hydrogen-exposed, embrittlement-sensitive environments. [ 4 ]

The primary cost driver in austenitic stainless steels is the nickel content, which simultaneously plays a key role in determining resistance to HE. For example, the austenitic stainless steel X2CrNi18-9 (AISI 304L, DIN EN 1.4307), which contains no molybdenum and approximately 5 mass pct less nickel than X2CrNiMo18-14-3, represents a more cost-effective alternative. However, this reduction in nickel content comes at the expense of decreased resistance to HE, making the material more susceptible to hydrogen-induced degradation. [ 5 ,  6 – 7 ]

One factor that contributes significantly to the increased susceptibility to HE with decreasing nickel content is the reduced thermodynamic stability of austenite, which promotes the formation of thermally or strain-induced martensite. This martensitic phase, due to its body-centered cubic (bcc) structure, is intrinsically more sensitive to HE and exhibits hydrogen diffusivity several orders of magnitude higher than that of austenite. The significantly enhanced hydrogen mobility facilitates rapid transport of hydrogen into stress-concentrated regions, such as crack tips or dislocation networks, thereby accelerating hydrogen-induced crack initiation and propagation. [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]

Egels  et al. [ 10 ]  found that the HE behavior of X2CrNi18-9 austenitic stainless steels is influenced not only by the nominal global chemical composition, but also by the segregation state of alloying elements. Steels with identical nominal compositions but produced via different processing routes—continuous casting and electroslag remelting—exhibited significant differences in HE susceptibility due to segregation phenomena. Using combined Energy-Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS) and Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the study demonstrated that nickel segregates in bands parallel to the rolling direction, leading to local variations in austenite stability. Two-dimensional maps of austenite stability revealed that deformation-induced martensite preferentially forms in Ni-depleted regions. These areas of reduced phase stability were also strongly associated with the initiation and propagation of hydrogen-induced surface cracks, underscoring a direct correlation between local chemical inhomogeneity and resistance to HE.

Recently, several studies have compared the HE susceptibility of austenitic stainless steels produced via additive manufacturing (AM) using the laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M) process with their conventionally manufactured counterparts. [ 1 , 11 ,  12 – 13 ]  PBF-LB/M is an AM technique in which metal powder is selectively melted layer by layer using a focused laser beam, enabling the fabrication of complex geometries with fine-scale microstructures.

Claeys  et al. [ 12 ]  investigated the HE sensitivity of conventionally processed (cold-rolled and annealed) and PBF-LB/M-processed 316L austenitic stainless steel, focusing on the effects of heat treatment and surface condition. While the 316L steel processed by PBF-LB/M exhibited increased hydrogen solubility and slightly reduced diffusivity compared to its conventionally manufactured counterpart, it demonstrated lower HE sensitivity. Heat treatment of AM samples decreased hydrogen solubility and increased diffusivity but did not significantly affect their HE resistance. Alvarez  et al. [ 11 ]  similarly examined the influence of processing on the HE behavior of 316L stainless steel produced both conventionally and via PBF-LB/M. In addition, they evaluated a post-processing condition involving hot isostatic pressing (HIP). While PBF-LB/M variants generally showed reduced ductility compared to conventionally manufactured steel under uncharged conditions at room temperature, hydrogen-charged PBF-LB/M samples—particularly those subjected to HIP—exhibited comparable or even superior resistance to HE. Notably, at – 50 °C, HIP- and PBF-LB/M-processed 316L demonstrated nearly twice the ductility of hydrogen-charged steel manufactured conventionally. Among other mechanisms, this enhanced performance was linked to the lower tendency of AM microstructures to form strain-induced martensite, particularly at sub-zero conditions.

Neither of the mentioned studies evaluated the influence of chemical homogeneity, which was identified by Egels  et al.  as a key factor affecting hydrogen embrittlement. To the best of the authors' knowledge, only one study has considered chemical homogeneity as a contributing factor to the superior HE resistance of additively manufactured materials compared to cast counterparts. Lee  et al. [ 14 ]  compared the HE resistance of the metastable austenitic steel X2CrNi18-9 in cast, cast and rolled, and PBF-LB/M conditions. They found that both the PBF-LB/M and cast and rolled materials showed significantly less ductility loss after hydrogen charging compared to the cast reference. The lower HE resistance of the cast material was correlated with a higher volume fraction of strain-induced martensite, which was attributed to reduced chemical homogeneity. This inhomogeneity was observed primarily in regions adjacent to retained  δ -ferrite after casting, characterized by elevated Cr and reduced Ni concentrations. As a result, these Ni-depleted areas exhibited lower austenite stability than suggested by the nominal composition, leading to a higher tendency for martensite formation. In contrast, the cast + rolled and PBF-LB/M conditions surprisingly showed no differences in chemical homogeneity in this study, which may be attributed to the limited sample area analyzed in the EDS investigations. This finding is particularly noteworthy, as it is well established that cast and subsequently deformed materials do exhibit mesoscopic segregations, which, as demonstrated by Egels  et al. , [ 10 ]  have a significant impact on hydrogen embrittlement resistance.

In contrast, the powder metallurgical processing route, including PBF-LB/M and HIP, is generally characterized by a high degree of chemical homogeneity, particularly at the mesoscale. This is primarily attributed to the atomization process used to produce the feedstock powder. Due to their small size, powder particles solidify rapidly and do not exhibit the segregation typically observed during the solidification of cast steel. This leads to the research hypothesis addressed in the present work:

“The enhanced chemical homogeneity of additively manufactured austenitic stainless steels, compared to that resulting from conventional manufacturing routes, reduces their tendency to form martensite when comparing steels of the same nominal chemical composition. This increase in local austenite stability is a key factor contributing to the higher HE resistance of powder metallurgically produced parts.”

This hypothesis is schematically illustrated in Figure  1 , which compares the resulting chemical homogeneity—specifically the nickel distribution—as well as the distribution of Δ G γ → α  (thermodynamic austenite stability) between the conventional manufacturing route and the powder metallurgical approaches, namely HIP and PBF-LB/M. Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of the research hypothesis

The research hypothesis is investigated in this work using an optimized X2CrNi18-9 (DIN EN 1.4307) steel, as published in Reference  15 . The optimization focused on enhancing the solidification-related chemical homogeneity typically observed in conventionally manufactured steels. This was achieved by combining automated Scheil–Gulliver solidification simulations with a multi-objective optimization algorithm. The objective was to tune the solidification sequence such that the chemical segregations of Cr and Ni due to primary delta-ferrite are minimized. For a detailed description of the optimization algorithm employed or the active boundary conditions, the reader is referred the original publication. [ 15 ]  Applied within the compositional range of DIN EN 1.4307, the approach enabled a significant improvement in the homogeneity of austenite stability in conventionally manufactured steel solely through targeted adjustments to the global alloy composition.

In the present work, the steel is examined in four different processing conditions: conventional casting followed by hot forming (low chemical homogeneity with typical equiaxed austenite grains) PBF-LB/M (high chemical homogeneity with a fine-grained microstructure characterized by high dislocation density and microsegregation) solution-annealed PBF-LB/M (reduced dislocation density and microsegregation compared to the as-built PBF-LB/M condition) HIP (high chemical homogeneity with typical equiaxed austenite grains)

The susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement was assessed indirectly by evaluating the tendency for martensitic phase transformation under low-temperature tensile loading, complemented by detailed microstructural investigations with a particular focus on chemical homogeneity.

sections.heading: Material Production
paragraphs: The material of steel grade X2CrNi18-9, whose chemical composition was optimized with regard to HE in Reference  15 , was produced using three different manufacturing routes. In the following, a distinction is made between: (1) Wrought (conventionally cast and hot worked), (2) PBF-LB/M, and (3) HIP.

sections.heading: Wrought
paragraphs: The wrought material was produced by melting a 3 kg ingot in a vacuum induction furnace (Leybold-Heraeus, Germany) under a 500 mbar argon atmosphere. The ingot was subsequently hot forged at 1100 °C using a round-die hammer, reducing its diameter from 42 to 12 mm over 6 forging steps. This corresponded to a forming strain of 42 pct per step and a total cumulative strain of 251 pct. The chemical composition was measured by optical emission spectrometry (OES) (OBLF QSG750).

sections.heading: Powder Production for (2) and (3)
paragraphs: The powder required for producing the PBF-LB/M and HIP specimens was manufactured using the vacuum induction melting inert gas atomization (VIGA) process, employing the AUG 3000 atomizer from Blue Power. The feedstock material was melted under an argon atmosphere at a pressure of 1.02 bar and a temperature of 1710 °C. Nitrogen was used as the atomization gas at a pressure of 30 bar, without pre-heating. After atomization, the powder was sieved and air-classified into particle size fractions of 20–63  µ m for PBF-LB/M and 63–150  µ m for HIP. To determine the chemical composition via OES, the powder was remelted in an MC 20 V furnace (Indutherm) using indirect induction heating via a graphite susceptor and an alumina crucible.

sections.heading: PBF-LB/M
paragraphs: PBF-LB/M processing was carried out using a TruPrint3000 system (TRUMPF GmbH). The processing parameters applied were as follows: laser power: 160 W, scan speed: 900 mm/s, layer thickness: 30   µ m, hatch distance: 80   µ m, process gas: N 2 , and scan strategy: stripes. The selection of these parameters was based on a preceding parameter study aimed at achieving the highest possible density in the produced specimens. The specimen geometry, which was later used for the fabrication of tensile test samples, was cylindrical with a diameter of 8 mm and a length of 60 mm. All specimens were manufactured in the horizontal build orientation, as shown in Figure  2 (b). Fig. 2 Schematic illustration of sampling position and orientation of the tensile specimens from ( a ) wrought, ( b ) PBF-LB/M, and ( c ) HIP, as well as the tensile specimen geometry ( d ) machined from the respective semi-finished products (a) through (c)

sections.heading: HIP
paragraphs: For HIP, the powder was initially hermetically sealed in a cylindrical capsule made of X5CrNi18-10 stainless steel, with a diameter of 60 mm and a height of 100 mm. The HIP process was carried out in a HIP unit of EPSI, model HIP 200 × 500 × 1500 mm 3 . The process parameters were set to a temperature of 1180 °C, a pressure of 1050 bar, and a holding time of 3 hours.

sections.heading: Tensile Testing
paragraphs: The sampling position and orientation of the tensile specimens from the wrought, PBF-LB/M, and HIP materials are shown in Figures  2 (a) through (c). The tensile specimen geometry used is shown in Figure  2 (d) and was machined by wet turning from the semi-finished products shown in Figures  2 (a) through (c). After machining, the wrought specimens, half of the PBF-LB/M specimens, and the HIP specimens were solution annealed in an industrial vacuum furnace (U 54/1 F, Schmetz) at 1050 °C for 60 minutes, followed by quenching with argon gas at a pressure of 200 kPa. This solution-annealing (SA) step was carried out to eliminate any potential effects of machining-induced martensite and N-uptake along the surfaces of the tensile samples. Based on this, the following material conditions were tested: (1) Wrought + SA, (2.1) PBF-LB/M, (2.2) PBF-LB/M + SA, and (3) HIP + SA. The reason for considering both the as-built and the solution-annealed conditions for PBF-LB/M was to investigate the influence of the characteristic PBF-LB/M microstructure, featuring high dislocation density, anisotropy, and fine grain size, on phase stability and mechanical behavior at low temperatures.

Tensile tests were performed using a Z100 universal testing machine from Zwick and Roell at a test temperature of − 50 °C in gaseous nitrogen. This temperature corresponds to the ductility minimum typically observed in austenitic steels [ 16 ]  and was therefore used as a worst-case scenario in the context of HE. The tensile tests were performed in accordance with ASTM G129, using an initial strain rate of 5.5 × 10 −5  s −1 . For each condition, three tensile specimens were tested, and the average values were calculated for elongation at fracture ( A ), uniform elongation ( A g ), yield strength ( R p0,2 ), and ultimate tensile strength ( R m ).

sections.heading: Microstructural Investigations
paragraphs: Microstructural analysis of the initial conditions was carried out using a MIRA 3 scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Tescan). Sample preparation included grinding (54, 18   µ m), polishing with diamond suspensions (3, 1   µ m), and electrolytic polishing to prevent preparation-induced martensite formation. For grain size determination according to the line-intercept method (ASTM E112-13), images were acquired at ×400 magnification using backscattered electron (BSE) contrast. An exception applies to the PBF-LB/M and PBF-LB/M + SA conditions, for which the grain size was determined using higher-magnification images due to the smaller grain size. For this purpose, the image area recorded at a magnification of ×400 was stitched from multiple images acquired at a magnification of ×2000. This procedure is exemplarily illustrated in Supplementary Figure  S-1 .

Microstructural analysis after tensile testing was performed on metallographic cross-sections prepared analogously to the procedure described above. To first reveal the largest possible areas, the samples were etched using Beraha-II and subsequently examined at different magnifications with a Leica optical microscope (OM) of type DM 6M.

In addition, EBSD analyses were carried out using the aforementioned SEM with the following parameters: acceleration voltage of 20 keV, working distance of 15 mm, sample tilt of 70 deg, binning of 4, and a step size of 0.2  µ m. The SEM is equipped with an energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS) detector from Oxford Instruments, which enabled simultaneous acquisition of the elemental distributions of Fe, Cr, and Ni during EBSD measurements.

Based on these quantitative element mappings and assuming constant C and N levels as measured by OES (see Section  II–A ), the Gibbs free energy difference between the austenitic and martensitic phases (Δ G γ → α ) was calculated using Thermo-Calc in combination with the TC-Python SDK. The calculations were performed at − 50 °C, corresponding to the tensile testing temperature. Chemical homogeneity was evaluated from the resulting Δ G  maps by generating histograms and determining the mean value, standard deviation ( σ ), interquartile range (IQR), and median absolute deviation (MAD).

The phase constitution and composition before and after tensile testing was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD). A Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer was used, employing Cu Kα  radiation (wavelength of 1.5406 Å) in Bragg–Brentano geometry. Measurements were performed in the 2 θ  range from 40 to 100 deg, with a step size of 0.01deg and an acquisition time of 3 seconds per step for the initial conditions and 5 seconds per step for the post-tensile specimens. The quantification of the austenitic and martensitic phase fractions was performed using the Rietveld method with the MAUD software. [ 17 ]  To eliminate any instrument-specific reflection broadening, the evaluation was calibrated with Al 2 O 2  powder (Crystallography Open Database [COD] card 1000032) with a grain size below 1  µ m. For the phase quantification, fcc iron (COD card 9008469) and bcc iron (COD card 9008536) were considered.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The following discussion focuses on the research hypothesis underlying this work, namely that the higher chemical homogeneity of powder-metallurgically produced grade X2CrNi18-9 (HIP and PBF-LB/M), compared to conventionally wrought material, enhances resistance to HE, primarily by mitigating the tendency for  α -martensite formation. To this end, the differences in mechanical properties observed in tensile tests at − 50 °C will be presented and subsequently correlated with the corresponding microstructural changes occurring during deformation. However, to reliably assess the influence of chemical homogeneity and the microstructures resulting from the different processing routes, it is first necessary to compare the macroscopic chemical compositions and the initial microstructure of the individual conditions.

sections.heading: Comparison of the Initial States
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the diffraction patterns of the different conditions recorded prior to tensile testing. All conditions exhibit only reflections of the fcc austenitic phase, indicating a fully austenitic phase state. In the solution-annealed conditions, this phase state is achieved by heat treatment at 1050 °C—where only the austenitic phase is stable—followed by water quenching (solution annealing). In contrast, in the PBF-LB/M condition, the formation of a fully austenitic microstructure results from the high solidification and cooling rates during processing. These conditions favor primary austenitic solidification over ferritic solidification and additionally suppress solid-state phase transformations. A fully austenitic phase condition of PBF-LB/M-produced X2CrNi18-9 has also been reported in other studies. [ 19 ,  20 ,  21 – 22 ]  A closer examination of the diffraction patterns in Figure  3  reveals that the  γ (220) reflection exhibits the highest intensity in the PBF-LB/M condition, whereas in the other conditions the  γ (111) reflection dominates. This is consistent with X-ray diffraction data of PBF-LB/M-processed 304L by Zhang  et al. [ 20 , 23 ]  Using additional EBSD measurements, they detected an <100> texture parallel to the build direction. This preferred orientation, commonly observed in PBF-LB/M-processed austenitic steels, is attributed to directional solidification driven by the steep temperature gradient between the melt pool center and the already solidified material or the underlying substrate. As a result, elongated grains grow from the melt pool boundary—often accompanied by epitaxial growth—toward the melt pool center,  i.e.,  in the negative direction of the maximum temperature gradient. PBF-LB/M microstructures are typically characterized by columnar grains with a distinctive cellular–dendritic substructure resulting from the high solidification and cooling rates. The latter exhibits elemental segregation, with higher concentrations of Cr and Ni in the cell boundaries than within the cells. This characteristic microstructure is also observed in the steel investigated in the present work and will be shown in the analysis of the initial microstructures. Fig. 3 XRD patterns obtained prior to tensile testing of X2CrNi18-9 in the different investigated conditions. PBF-LB/M and PBF-LB/M + SA samples were analyzed parallel to the build direction

Figure  4  shows a comparison of the microstructures of grade X2CrNi18-9 in the different conditions prior to tensile testing. Figure  4 (c), which shows the microstructure of the PBF-LB/M condition parallel to the build direction, confirms columnar grains aligned along the build direction. In addition, the close-up image in the upper corner of Figure  4 (c) illustrates the characteristic cellular substructure. Not only the columnar grain morphology but also the average grain size of 9.5   µ m distinguishes the PBF-LB/M condition from the Wrought + SA [Figure  4 (a)] and HIP + SA [Figure  4 (b)] conditions. Both exhibit significantly larger grain sizes of 27.7   µ m (Wrought + SA) and 15.8   µ m (HIP + SA), respectively. In addition, they reveal the typical microstructure of conventionally produced austenitic steels, consisting of equiaxed grains interspersed with a few twin grain boundaries. Examination of the micrograph of the PBF-LB/M + SA condition with an average grain size of 8.2   µ m in Figure  4 (d) shows that a subsequent one-hour heat treatment at 1050 °C does not exert a significant influence on the grain structure of the PBF-LB/M condition. The slight reduction in grain size could be attributed to recrystallization, which was detected by Zhang  et al. [ 19 ]  after a 2-hour solution annealing treatment at 1050 °C of PBF-LB/M-produced X2CrNi18-9. This hypothesis is contradicted by the absence of recrystallization twins in the PBF-LB/M + SA condition, as shown in Supplementary Figure S-1. Therefore, it is assumed that recrystallization processes play only a subordinate role and that the slightly smaller grain size observed in the PBF-LB/M + SA condition lies within the measurement uncertainty of the line-intercept method. Accordingly, it is concluded that the grain size is not, or not significantly, altered by the subsequent solution annealing treatment. Zhang  et al. [ 19 ]  also demonstrated that the cellular segregation structure formed due to the high solidification and cooling rates in the PBF-LB/M process was dissolved during annealing. Fig. 4 SEM images of the initial states ( BD  build direction)

The detected differences in grain size directly affect the  M d30  temperature according to Eq. [ 1 ]. Therefore, Table  I  lists not only the  M d30  temperature calculated solely from the chemical composition but also the values calculated with consideration of grain size. It is evident that smaller grain sizes shift the  M d30  temperature toward lower. As a result, the  M d30  temperatures of the PM conditions approach that of the Wrought + SA condition, but do not reach it. Thus, even when grain size is considered, the Wrought + SA condition exhibits the lowest tendency for martensite formation among all conditions, at least as indicated by the  M d30  temperature and based on the global chemical composition.

sections.heading: Comparison of Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Figure  5 (a) shows representative stress–strain curves obtained from tensile tests at − 50 °C for grade X2CrNi18-9 in the different investigated conditions. The respective mechanical properties are listed in Table  II  and are graphically shown in Figure  5 (b). The PBF-LB/M condition exhibits the highest yield strength (489 MPa) and ultimate tensile strength (684 MPa), but also the lowest elongation at fracture (67.1 pct). Subsequent solution annealing of the PBF-LB/M condition results in a relative decrease in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength by 34 and 10 pct, respectively, while the elongation at fracture increases by 14 pct. The effect of post-process solution annealing on the mechanical properties of steels manufactured by PBF-LB/M has been reported in the literature. Zhang  et al. [ 19 ]  found that solution annealing at 1050 °C of PBF-LB/M-processed X2CrNi18-9 stainless steel led, on the one hand, to an overall reduction in dislocation density, while on the other hand dislocations within the cellular walls dissociated and migrated to energetically favorable regions, forming subgrain boundaries with locally increased dislocation density. This resulted in a decrease in strength accompanied by an increase in elongation. [ 19 ] Fig. 5 ( a ) Representative stress–strain curves of the different investigated conditions; ( b ) graphical representation of the characteristic mechanical properties obtained from tensile testing Table II Mechanical Properties from Tensile Testing at − 50 °C Condition Yield Strength in MPa Ultimate Strength in MPa Uniform Elongation in Pct Elongation at Fracture in Pct Wrought + SA 162 ± 24 658 ± 55 67.9 ± 1.6 80.2 ± 1.0 HIP + SA 236 ± 2 630 ± 17 76.4 ± 3.4 89.8 ± 3.6 PBF-LB/M 489 ± 11 684 ± 17 52.4 ± 3.8 67.1 ± 4.3 PBF-LB/M + SA 347 ± 37 619 ± 24 63.4 ± 5.6 76.7 ± 4.6

The HIP + SA condition shows the highest values of uniform elongation and elongation at fracture, indicating the most ductile material behavior among all conditions. The yield strength of the HIP + SA condition lies between that of the PBF-LB/M + SA and the Wrought + SA conditions. The latter exhibits a significantly lower average yield strength of 162 MPa compared to the PM conditions, while its ultimate tensile strength of 658 MPa approaches the highest value observed for the PBF-LB/M condition. Furthermore, the uniform and fracture elongations of the Wrought + SA condition are 5 to 7 pct higher than in the PBF-LB/M + SA condition but approximately 12 pct lower than in the HIP + SA condition.

The comparison of the mechanical properties already reveals considerable differences between the investigated conditions. In addition, two distinct types of plastic deformation can be identified. The PM conditions HIP + SA, PBF-LB/M, and PBF-LB/M + SA exhibit a parabolic curve shape, whereas the Wrought + SA condition displays a sigmoidal progression. This difference already points to distinct deformation mechanisms active during tensile testing of the respective conditions. Generally, the activation of these mechanisms is primarily governed by the stacking fault energy (SFE). In high-SFE steels, deformation predominantly proceeds via dislocation glide. Accordingly, the strain-hardening rate d σ true /d ε true , defined as the slope of the true stress–strain curve, decreases continuously after reaching a maximum in the strain range of the yield point. This behavior, evident in the HIP + SA, PBF-LB/M + SA, and PBF-LB/M conditions, is shown in the strain-hardening curves in Figure  6 , which display a steadily decreasing strain hardening rate with increasing true strain, resulting in parabolic engineering stress–strain curves. In steels with lower SFE, deformation increasingly occurs by twinning and by phase transformations to  ε - and  α -martensite, also known as transformation induced plasticity (TRIP). Both deformation modes lead to pronounced strain hardening and, depending on their extent, may give rise to plateaus or local maxima in the strain-hardening rate within the range of uniform elongation. [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ]  This behavior, and thus pronounced strain hardening, is evident for the Wrought + SA condition in the strain-hardening curve shown in Figure  6 (a). It is further corroborated by the highest true uniform strain—corresponding to the true strain at the onset of necking—determined as 0.53 for the Wrought + SA condition by application of the Considère criterion [ 27 ]  (Figure  6 ). Fig. 6 True stress-strain curves and strain hardening rate curves

These results already point to markedly different deformation behavior of the PM conditions compared to the conventionally manufactured condition, despite their almost identical macroscopic chemical composition and, consequently, similar SFE.

sections.heading: Microstructure and Phase Constitution After Tensile Testing
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows OM images of Beraha-II-etched cross-sections of tensile specimens tested at − 50 °C at different magnifications. In this etching, the austenitic phase appears bright, while the martensitic phase is revealed in a brownish-dark contrast. However, shear bands, which are not necessarily martensitic, also appear dark, which prevents an exact quantitative assessment of the martensite content. Nevertheless, the images provide a first impression of the retained austenite as well as its constitution and morphology. Fig. 7 OM micrographs at different magnifications after tensile testing in Beraha-ll etched state

At the lowest magnification in Figures  7 (a1), through (d1), it becomes evident that the austenitic phase differs in content, morphology, and size among the investigated conditions. The austenite fraction is lowest in the Wrought + SA condition and highest in the HIP + SA condition, while the PBF-LB/M and PBF-LB/M + SA conditions lie in between. This qualitative impression is confirmed by the diffraction patterns of the tensile-tested specimens shown in Figure  8 . Rietveld analysis yielded the following martensitic and austenitic phase fractions: Wrought + SA: 54 vol pct martensite (46 vol pct austenite); HIP + SA: 9 vol pct martensite (91 vol pct austenite); PBF-LB/M: 33 vol pct martensite (67 vol pct austenite); and PBF-LB/M + SA: 37 vol pct martensite (63 vol pct austenite). This confirms the lower transformation tendency of the PBF-LB/M condition compared to its conventional counterpart, as reported in the literature (see Section  I ). Besides, the HIP condition exhibits the lowest tendency for martensitic phase transformation. It should be noted that the α-martensite fractions detected here were not measured at identical plastic deformation states due to the different elongations achieved. For example, the measured α-martensite fraction in the PBF-LB/M condition corresponds to a state of lower plastic deformation compared to the HIP + SA condition. However, this has only a minor impact on addressing the research hypothesis, as indicated by the strain hardening data. Fig. 8 XRD patterns obtained after tensile testing

In addition to the fraction of strain-induced martensite, Figure  7  also reveals differences in the constitution, size, and distribution of the austenitic and martensitic phase regions. In general, three types can be distinguished: (1) fully retained austenite grains, (2) austenite grains intersected by shear bands (martensite in shear bands is not recognizable), and (3) austenite grains with clearly recognizable martensite within the shear bands. While regions of types 1 and 2 predominate in the HIP + SA condition, a significantly larger fraction of type 3 regions is observed in the Wrought + SA, PBF-LB/M, and PBF-LB/M + SA conditions, with the width of the martensitic shear bands varying significantly within one single condition.

While no clear differences can be detected between the PBF-LB/M and PBF-LB/M + SA conditions, a pronounced difference is observed between the PBF-LB/M conditions and the Wrought + SA condition with respect to the size and arrangement of the different regions. In general, it exhibits a much finer deformation microstructure than the additively manufactured steels. This applies both to the fully retained austenitic grains (type 1) and to the regions intersected by martensitic shear bands (type 3).

The EBSD analyses performed near the necking region of the specimens, as shown in Figure  9 , provide additional insights into the spatial distribution of the phases. In contrast to the OM micrographs in Figure  7 , which correspond to a region of uniform elongation, the EBSD results for the Wrought + SA condition reveal austenitic and martensitic phases arranged in rows parallel to the deformation direction, which also coincided with the tensile loading direction. In the HIP condition, the predominantly austenitic state is confirmed, with martensite appearing as needle-like features extending across entire austenite grains. The PBF-LB/M and PBF-LB/M + SA conditions show significant differences in the EBSD analyses, which can be attributed to the fact that the magnification selected here is not sufficient to adequately capture the coarser transformation microstructure of the PBF-LB/M conditions revealed by the Beraha-ll etching and lower magnifications in Figure  7 . Thus, for the PBF-LB/M condition, an area with a high martensite fraction was analyzed, whereas for the PBF-LB/M + SA condition, the region analyzed contained locally more austenite. This underlines the importance of scale-dependent microstructural analysis of deformation structures and highlights that examining areas that are too small may lead to misinterpretations regarding the resulting phase fractions. For this reason, the OM images at low magnification, in combination with the X-ray investigations, are of great significance for the interpretation of the results in this work. As described in Section  II–C , elemental maps were acquired simultaneously with the EBSD measurements using EDS to correlate the phase transformation tendency with the local chemical composition. For these investigations, the magnification shown here was chosen based on the work of Egels  et al. , [ 10 ]  as it allows the heterogeneous elemental distribution of the conventionally manufactured material to be visualized. The correlation between mechanical properties, α-martensite content, and chemical homogeneity is discussed in the next section. sections.heading: Correlation Between Mechanical Properties,  α -Martensite Content and Chemical Homogeneity
paragraphs: Clear differences in the mechanical properties, microstructures, and in particular the fraction of deformation-induced martensite after tensile testing at – 50 °C have been observed among the differently processed variants of steel X2CrNi18-9. Two key findings may be summarized at this point: The Wrought + SA condition is the only one to exhibit a second maximum in the strain-hardening rate during tensile testing, indicating pronounced work hardening during deformation. The Wrought + SA condition shows the highest fraction of strain-induced martensite after tensile testing. This martensite is aligned in bands along the deformation direction in the vicinity of the necking region.

Based on these two findings, it can be concluded that deformation-induced martensite formation in the Wrought + SA material contributed significantly to strain hardening during tensile testing, leading to a sigmoidal stress-strain curve. In contrast, the parabolic stress–strain curves of the PM conditions can be attributed to the lower α-martensite content, which is assumed to form only at higher strains and therefore does not contribute to strain hardening,  i.e.,  the occurrence of a maximum in the strain-hardening rate (see Figure  6 ). The extreme case is represented by the HIP + SA condition, in which the lowest martensite content was detected; hence, deformation in this condition proceeds predominantly by dislocation glide.

According to the research hypothesis, this significantly different behavior is now to be examined based on chemical homogeneity. Figures  10 (a) through (c) shows the elemental maps of Fe, Cr, and Ni for the Wrought + SA condition, corresponding to the microstructural region analyzed by EBSD in Figures  9 (a1) through (a3). These reveal a band-like segregation structure of Fe, Cr and, in particular, Ni, which corresponds to the band-like arrangement of the austenitic and martensitic phase fractions shown in Figure  9 (a3). It also becomes evident that Fe and Cr exhibit a segregation behavior opposite to that of Ni, meaning that higher Fe and Cr contents are measured in regions of lower Ni concentration. This opposite segregation behavior can be attributed to the solidification of the melt during casting. Primary ferritic solidification occurs, characterized by an intrinsically higher solubility for Cr and a lower solubility for Ni. As a result, Ni segregates into the remaining liquid phase, where it contributes to the austenitic solidification of the residual liquid. Fig. 10 ( a ) through ( c ) Elemental distributions of Fe, Cr, and Ni in the Wrought + SA condition measured by EDS; resulting Δ G γ → α  maps of ( d ) Wrought + SA, ( e ) HIP + SA, ( f ) PBF-LB/M, and ( g ) PBF-LB/M + SA

Figure  10 (d) shows the Δ G γ→ α  map of the Wrought + SA condition calculated from the elemental maps. In principle, it would also be possible to represent the distribution of the  M d30  temperature. However, it is the austenite phase stability which, according to the description of Talonen  et al. , [ 28 ]  in combination with the SFE, influences the transformation behavior through the critical size of α-martensite embryos during nucleation. The higher the austenite stability— i.e.,  the higher the required driving force for transformation into α-martensite—the larger the critical size of the α-martensite embryos. Since austenite stability is determined primarily by the chemical composition, it is used here as the relevant parameter in the maps, whereas  M d30  also incorporates grain size effects that cannot be accounted for in terms of the local chemical composition.

Consistent with the band-like segregations, the Δ G γ → α  map of the Wrought + SA condition in Figure  10 (d) reveals corresponding variations in local austenite stability. Regions with elevated Ni concentrations exhibit higher Δ G γ → α  values and, consequently, locally increased austenite stability. It is precisely these regions that remain austenitic in the microstructure during tensile testing [see Figure  9 (a3)], whereas the regions with lower Ni content and thus lower austenite stability transform completely into martensite. For the PM conditions HIP + SA, PBF-LB/M, and PBF-LB/M + SA, only the Δ G γ → α  maps calculated from the elemental maps are shown, as no apparent variations in the local elemental distribution could be detected. This is reflected in the homogeneous Δ G γ → α  distribution visible in the maps in Figures  10 (e) through (g). Thus, it is apparent that the chemical homogeneity in the PM conditions is higher than in the Wrought + SA condition.

To substantiate this statement with quantitative values, the data from the Δ G γ → α  maps were further evaluated statistically. Figure  11  shows histograms of Δ G γ → α  for the different conditions, obtained from the maps in Figure  10 . The mean Δ G γ → α  ( µ ), and thus the average thermodynamic austenite stability, is highest in the Wrought + SA condition. This result is consistent with the  M d30  temperatures in Table  I  and can be attributed to the slight deviation in chemical composition discussed in Section  III–A  and shown in Table  I . The higher values of standard deviation ( σ ), IQR, and MAD for the Wrought + SA material clearly indicate a larger scatter in Δ G γ → α , which directly correlates with lower chemical homogeneity. This means that the frequency of regions with low austenite stability is higher than in the PM conditions, thereby providing larger areas that serve as favorable sites for  α -martensite nucleation and formation. However, comparison of the phase distribution map in Figure  9 (a3) with the Δ G γ → α  distribution in Figure  10 (d) for the Wrought + SA condition also shows that deformation-induced martensite extends into regions of high austenite stability, similar to those observed in the PM conditions. In other words, in the Wrought + SA condition, regions with Δ G γ → α  values comparable to those of the PM conditions, which remain austenitic in the latter, undergo transformation. This may be attributed to the rapid burst-like growth of  α -martensite beyond the boundaries of shear bands, which, according to Hedström  et al. , [ 29 ]  can be understood as an autocatalytic process. The growth of α-martensite is initially triggered by externally applied stresses, but the volume expansion associated with the  γ  →  α  transformation generates additional stresses that, in a chain-reaction-like manner, further promote the  γ  →  α  transformation. This autocatalytic growth could explain why even a few or small regions of reduced austenite stability can result in a significantly higher α-martensite fraction in the Wrought + SA condition compared to the PM conditions. Fig. 11 Histograms of Δ G γ → α  distributions obtained from Figure  10 , with  μ  mean,  σ  standard deviation,  IQR  interquartile range, and  MAD  median absolute deviation

Comparison of the histograms of the PM conditions, and in particular the HIP + SA condition with the two PBF-LB/M conditions, shows that the HIP + SA condition exhibits slightly lower chemical homogeneity than the PBF-LB/M conditions, yet nevertheless displays a significantly lower tendency for martensitic phase transformation. The difference in martensitic phase fraction between PBF-LB/M and HIP can therefore not be explained by chemical homogeneity. The significantly higher martensite fractions observed in the PBF-LB/M conditions after tensile testing may be attributed to their texture. It is well established that shear bands, which act as nucleation sites for α-martensite, form preferentially in grains oriented close to <111> or <101> relative to the loading direction. [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]  Accordingly, a texture that promotes such favorable orientations increases the density of nucleation sites and can thus increase the α-martensite fraction. The <100> texture parallel to the build direction in the PBF-LB/M condition, reported by Zhang  et al. [ 19 ]  and briefly addressed in Section  III-A , was shown to remain unchanged during solution annealing. This persistence is consistent with the similar microstructures of the PBF-LB/M conditions observed in the SEM images in Figure  4 . Texture-driven martensite formation could therefore explain the comparable martensite fractions observed after tensile testing for both PBF-LB/M conditions. Moreover, a <100> texture oriented perpendicular to the loading direction may increase the tendency for martensite formation compared to vertically built samples, where the <100> texture is aligned with the tensile axis. A detailed investigation of this hypothesis is beyond the scope of this work and should be addressed in future studies, for instance by manufacturing and testing tensile specimens with different build-platform orientations in PBF-LB/M process.

The results demonstrate that PM-produced X2CrNi18-9, whether in the PBF-LB/M or HIP condition, exhibits a lower tendency for α-martensite formation during tensile testing at − 50 °C compared to the conventionally manufactured condition. The results of this work show that chemical homogeneity plays a decisive role in this context. As outlined in Section  I , however, the literature has either not addressed this aspect at all or has considered it only insufficiently when discussing the HE resistance of additively manufactured steels compared to their conventionally produced counterparts. The results of this work should therefore motivate the inclusion of chemical homogeneity, alongside other factors, as a variable influencing HE. Furthermore, these findings open up potential avenues for alloy design of stainless steels manufactured by PM for use in hydrogen environments. Specifically, the lower transformation tendency of PM microstructures could allow for a reduction in Ni content, which would have both ecological and economic benefits for the alloy.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The present work shows that the lower chemical homogeneity of conventionally manufactured metastable austenitic steel X2CrNi18-9 results in a higher fraction of deformation-induced martensite during tensile testing at − 50 °C compared to PM-produced variants manufactured by PBF-LB/M or HIP. This work therefore introduces chemical homogeneity as a significant factor contributing to the improved HE resistance of PM-produced steels reported in the literature.

The following conclusions can be drawn: In conventionally manufactured X2CrNi18-9 (cast and hot-formed), segregations of Cr and Ni are observed within bands aligned parallel to the deformation direction. Regions with lower Ni content transform preferentially due to the locally reduced austenite stability. The martensitic transformation also extends into regions of higher austenite stability, which has been attributed to an autocatalytic burst-like growth mechanism. The chemical homogeneity, and thus the uniformity of austenite stability, is higher in the PM conditions. This implies a lower density of favorable nucleation sites for martensite formation compared to the conventionally manufactured material, resulting in a smaller fraction of strain-induced martensite. Although the chemical homogeneity of the PBF-LB/M and HIP conditions is comparable, the PBF-LB/M conditions in both the as-built and solution-annealed states exhibit a higher fraction of deformation-induced martensite. The texture of the PBF-LB/M conditions has been proposed as a possible explanation, which remains to be investigated in future work.
